A Colombian chef, Oscar Rosas, has recounted how he was allegedly held captive for three years by a criminal gang in Bogotá and forced to cook and eat human flesh for drug dealers and international criminals. 61 years old Rosas said members of the Los Sayayines gang abducted him after he accepted an offer to prepare meals for an underground gathering in exchange for heroin and crack cocaine. According to the Daily Mail, which published an interview with him on November 15, Rosas said he was living in El Bronx, a notorious drug-dealing district in the Colombian capital, when the gang approached him with the offer. He said his life had deteriorated following a heroin addiction that ended his career as a chef, despite having received culinary training in New York and worked in restaurants across Europe. After returning to Colombia, he eventually found himself living on the streets of El Bronx, where criminal gangs controlled drug activities and other operations. Rosas said the gang promised him drugs in exchange for preparing food for a private gathering attended by people from different parts of the world. “They had silverware, and good wines and champagne. They said they were bringing guests from all over the world. I said I’d make them whatever they want, and they said they would pay me back in heroin. They got me everything I needed,” he told the Daily Mail. He said he was taken underground, where he encountered a woman holding a dead chicken and was subjected to what he described as a ritual. “I went down into the tunnel, and there was a beautiful woman to my left. She was holding a dead chicken, and she wiped its blood on me and threw snails on me,” he said. According to Rosas, a gang member subsequently assaulted him and told him he would not be allowed to leave. “I said, ‘What are you doing? It’s me; you told me to come’, and he said, ‘I don’t care who you are; you are never getting out of here’,” he recalled. He said the gang member demanded that he perform a ritual, threatening to kill him if he refused. Rosas said the gang later brought a plastic bag containing human remains and ordered him to prepare the contents for the gathering. “They made me pick up a plastic bag full of meat they brought down with them and put it on the dinner table. “I grabbed it, I opened it, and they made me serve its contents on a gold platter,” he said. Rosas said he eventually prepared the remains as a stew after being threatened with death. “I felt like throwing up…I just remember putting the knife into that dismembered body, and prepped it as it were for a stew…It was the hardest thing I’ve ever had to do in my life,” he said. He further claimed that the gang forced him to taste the food and continued making him consume human flesh throughout his captivity. “I survived the first ritual…They made me take a bite….and for the next three years all I ate was human meat. “They wouldn’t let me eat anything else. I had no other choice. I had to do it,” he said. Rosas also alleged that he was made to remove organs from human bodies, particularly kidneys, in exchange for crack cocaine. “And every day there was a ritual…And they’d ask me to remove someone’s kidney…in exchange for crack,” he said. He claimed that men wearing coats arrived every few days carrying suitcases to collect the organs. “There was organ trafficking going on; it was the most horrible thing,” he said. Rosas alleged that the gatherings attracted members of guerrilla groups, paramilitary organisations, drug dealers, gang leaders and other international criminals. “Everyone who was down there would also eat the human bodies…they did it as a ritual, to protect their souls…by kidnapping their souls…” “People who did it were members of the guerrilla, paramilitaries, thieves, international criminals, drug dealers and powerful gang bosses,” he told the Daily Mail. He also claimed that criminals travelled from different parts of the world to participate in the gatherings. He said, “International criminals from all over the world would come to eat human flesh…in the form of a stew.” According to Rosas, the gang had access to several bodies, some of which he said came from killings and drug overdoses. “In that slum, we were never short of dead bodies. Some days we had seven or eight bodies coming through. “Sometimes they had been killed, others died of drug overdoses, some were members of the police…,” he said. Rosas said he remained in captivity for about three years before attempting suicide with a broken glass bottle. He said that while he was bleeding, he overheard members of the gang discussing plans to put him in an acid bath. “As I bled, I heard people saying to prepare an acid bath to put me in, but one of the Sayayines grabbed me and led me out of the tunnel, and dumped me on the street,” he said. He said he did not know why the gang member decided to release him. After being found by the police, Rosas was taken to hospital for treatment. He said medical personnel did not believe his account of what happened during his captivity and transferred him to a mental health ward. “No one believed me; they thought I was crazy. “I contemplated suicide….I didn’t want to face reality, plus, no one believed me,” he said. He said his situation improved after Christian volunteers began visiting him in hospital, where they prayed with him and introduced him to Christianity. “They would sit with me, they would pray with me, they taught me about God. “I still have my demons, but I finally feel peace,” he said. Rosas, who said he has been sober for 11 years, now lives in Bucaramanga, Colombia, where he runs a rehabilitation facility for people battling drug addiction. The Daily Mail reported that El Bronx was dismantled by Colombian security forces in 2016 following an operation involving more than 2,500 police officers and heavily armed soldiers. The operation led to the removal of more than 1,000 homeless people and drug users from the area, while about 130 minors were rescued. Some of the children were suspected of having been exploited in prostitution. Security operatives also arrested dozens of people and seized cocaine, marijuana and crack cocaine. Authorities subsequently discovered a 100-metre underground tunnel beneath a building occupied by squatters. The passage was reportedly used by criminal gangs to move drugs, weapons and kidnapping victims. The newspaper also reported that Juliana Quitana, then head of Colombia’s judicial police, said earlier in 2026 that there was sufficient evidence to suggest that criminal gangs had used murder victims to “feed homeless people” and “lure foreigners with cannibalistic tendencies”.
